items.stem: Why is the same restriction enzyme used to cut both the plasmid and the gene?
items.answer: To produce matching sticky ends that can pair up
items.markingKey: To produce matching sticky ends that can pair up. Complementary base pairing.

items.stem: Distinguish between a chromosome and a plasmid.
items.answer: A plasmid is a small circular extra piece of DNA in bacteria that can transfer between cells; a chromosome is the main DNA carrying most of the organism’s genes.
items.markingKey: A plasmid is a small circular extra piece of DNA in bacteria that can transfer between cells; a chromosome is the main DNA carrying most of the organism’s genes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Genetic engineering creates new genes from nothing." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It moves existing genes between organisms (or edits them); it does not create genes from nothing.
items.markingKey: It moves existing genes between organisms (or edits them); it does not create genes from nothing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Tomás counted transformed colonies when different masses of plasmid DNA were used (three plates each).

Mass of plasmid / ng | Colonies: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 42 | 42 | 42
20 | 71 | 72 | 72
40 | 117 | 115 | 112
80 | 164 | 156 | 164
160 | 202 | 204 | 213

Calculate the mean colonies when the mass of plasmid was 80 ng.
items.markingKey: M1 (164 + 156 + 164) ÷ 3; A1 161.3 (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Diego is investigating how the temperature of the heat-shock step affects the number of E. coli K-12 cells that take up a plasmid carrying a fluorescence gene. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: heat-shock temperature (37, 42, 47, 52 °C for 50 s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: heat-shock temperature (37, 42, 47, 52 °C for 50 s) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Describe the steps used to produce human insulin using genetically modified bacteria.
items.answer: Identify insulin gene; cut it out with a restriction enzyme (sticky ends); cut plasmid with the same enzyme; mix and join with DNA ligase → recombinant plasmid; insert into bacteria (transformation, e.g. heat shock); grow on antibiotic agar to select transformed bacteria (marker gene); culture in large fermenters with controlled pH, temperature, nutrients, oxygen; extract and purify insulin.
items.markingKey: Identify insulin gene; cut it out with a restriction enzyme (sticky ends); cut plasmid with the same enzyme; mix and join with DNA ligase → recombinant plasmid; insert into bacteria (transformation, e.g. heat shock); grow on antibiotic agar to select transformed bacteria (marker gene); culture in large fermenters with controlled pH, temperature, nutrients, oxygen; extract and purify insulin.

items.stem: Define the term "genetic engineering".
items.answer: Changing the genome of an organism by inserting a gene from another organism
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: changing the genome of an organism by inserting a gene from another organism. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why genetically engineered insulin is better than insulin from pigs.
items.answer: It is identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic reactions; supply is unlimited and not affected by animal supply or religious objections.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic reactions; supply is unlimited and not affected by animal supply or religious objections. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Bacteria that make human insulin are part human." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They carry one human gene; the rest of their DNA is bacterial.
items.markingKey: They carry one human gene; the rest of their DNA is bacterial. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a plasmid and a chromosome.
items.answer: A plasmid is a small circular extra piece of DNA in bacteria that can transfer between cells; a chromosome is the main DNA carrying most of the organism’s genes.
items.markingKey: A plasmid is a small circular extra piece of DNA in bacteria that can transfer between cells; a chromosome is the main DNA carrying most of the organism’s genes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In a bacterial transformation, 250 colonies grew on antibiotic agar after using 0.1 µg of plasmid DNA. Calculate the transformation efficiency in colonies per µg and explain why only transformed bacteria grow.
items.answer: 2500 colonies per µg; only bacteria with the plasmid carry the antibiotic-resistance marker gene
items.markingKey: M1 250 ÷ 0.1; A1 2500 per µg; B1 marker gene gives resistance – untransformed bacteria are killed.

items.stem: Using CRISPR-Cas9 (Doudna and Charpentier, 2012) as an example, explain new tools for genetic engineering.
items.answer: A bacterial defence system was adapted to cut DNA at almost any chosen sequence, allowing precise gene editing. Nobel Prize 2020; used to develop treatments for sickle-cell disease, but raises ethical questions about editing human embryos.
items.markingKey: Context (A bacterial defence system was adapted to cut DNA at almost any chosen sequence, allowing precise gene editing.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Nobel Prize 2020; used to develop treatments for sickle-cell disease, but raises ethical questions about editing human embryos. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to new tools for genetic engineering.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Gene editing with CRISPR should be allowed to correct genetic diseases in human embryos."
items.answer: Research should continue, but heritable embryo editing should wait for proven safety and broad social agreement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: could eliminate severe inherited diseases (e.g. Huntington’s); prevents suffering in future generations. Arguments against: changes are inherited by all descendants – unknown long-term effects; off-target edits; could lead to “designer babies” and inequality. Supported judgement: Research should continue, but heritable embryo editing should wait for proven safety and broad social agreement. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Aiko plans an investigation into how the temperature of the heat-shock step affects the number of E. coli K-12 cells that take up a plasmid carrying a fluorescence gene. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (heat-shock temperature (37, 42, 47, 52 °C for 50 s)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Growing one crop variety over a large area"?
options: monoculture
informed consent
vector
patent
items.answer: monoculture
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of monoculture.

items.stem: "GM crops are always bad for the environment." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some reduce pesticide use and allow less tillage, but others may encourage more herbicide use; effects depend on the crop and management.
items.markingKey: Some reduce pesticide use and allow less tillage, but others may encourage more herbicide use; effects depend on the crop and management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between genetic modification and selective breeding.
items.answer: Genetic modification transfers specific genes, even between species, in one generation; selective breeding chooses parents with desired traits over many generations within a species.
items.markingKey: Genetic modification transfers specific genes, even between species, in one generation; selective breeding chooses parents with desired traits over many generations within a species. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Aiko used farm data on the mass of insecticide sprayed per hectare on cotton in years after Bt cotton was introduced (three regions).

Years after introduction | Insecticide used / kg/ha: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 2.86 | 2.81 | 2.81
2 | 1.96 | 1.92 | 1.87
4 | 1.42 | 1.41 | 1.33
6 | 1.04 | 1.06 | 1.04
8 | 0.85 | 0.85 | 0.85

State the years after introduction at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 2; range = 0.09 kg/ha; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 2; 1 range = max − min = 1.96 − 1.87 = 0.09 kg/ha; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Nia is investigating whether pollen from a GM maize field transfers the modified gene to non-GM maize at different distances. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the distance increases, then the percentage of GM-positive kernels will decrease, because less pollen reaches plants further away.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the distance increases, then the percentage of GM-positive kernels will decrease, because less pollen reaches plants further away.

items.stem: Amara investigated whether pollen from a GM maize field transfers the modified gene to non-GM maize at different distances. The method had this weakness: upwind and downwind plots were mixed together in the results. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: record wind direction and compare only plots in the same direction
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: record wind direction and compare only plots in the same direction

items.stem: How does Bt cotton reduce pesticide use?
options: It is poisonous to humans
It repels all animals
The plant makes its own insecticidal toxin
It grows faster than pests
items.answer: The plant makes its own insecticidal toxin
items.markingKey: C. The toxin targets certain caterpillars.

items.stem: Explain why insects may evolve resistance to Bt crops.
items.answer: Random mutations give some insects resistance; they survive on Bt crops and reproduce, so resistance spreads – which is why refuges of non-Bt crops are planted.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random mutations give some insects resistance; they survive on Bt crops and reproduce, so resistance spreads – which is why refuges of non-Bt crops are planted. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a Bt crop and a herbicide-resistant crop.
items.answer: A Bt crop produces its own insecticide; a herbicide-resistant crop survives being sprayed with weedkiller, so weeds can be killed.
items.markingKey: A Bt crop produces its own insecticide; a herbicide-resistant crop survives being sprayed with weedkiller, so weeds can be killed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Bt cotton in India (from 2002) shows benefits and limits of GM crops.
items.answer: Bt cotton spread to over 90% of India’s cotton area; yields rose and insecticide use fell at first, but pink bollworm later evolved resistance. It shows both the benefits of GM traits and how evolution can reduce them without careful management.
items.markingKey: Context (Bt cotton spread to over 90% of India’s cotton area; yields rose and insecticide use fell at first, but pink bollworm later evolved resistance.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows both the benefits of GM traits and how evolution can reduce them without careful management. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to benefits and limits of GM crops.

items.stem:
Diego used farm data on the mass of insecticide sprayed per hectare on cotton in years after Bt cotton was introduced (three regions).

Years after introduction | Insecticide used / kg/ha: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 3.14 | 3.07 | 3.04
2 | 2.16 | 2.24 | 2.24
4 | 1.52 | 1.54 | 1.56
6 | 1.15 | 1.15 | 1.16
8 | 0.94 | 0.98 | 0.99

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Insecticide use decreased after Bt cotton was introduced, rapidly at first and then levelling off. Bt cotton produces its own toxin against bollworms, so farmers needed to spray less; some spraying continues for other pests (and later for resistant pests).
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Insecticide use decreased after Bt cotton was introduced, rapidly at first and then levelling off.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Bt cotton produces its own toxin against bollworms, so farmers needed to spray less; some spraying continues for other pests (and later for resistant pests).

items.stem:
Omar is investigating whether pollen from a GM maize field transfers the modified gene to non-GM maize at different distances.
(a) State the independent variable. [1]
(b) State the dependent variable and how it will be measured. [1]
(c) Identify two control variables and explain why each must be kept constant. [2]
(d) Formulate a testable hypothesis and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
items.answer: (a) distance of the non-GM maize plot from the GM field (5, 25, 50, 100, 200 m). (b) percentage of kernels that test positive for the GM gene. (c) the same test kit – test sensitivity varies; number of cobs sampled per plot (20) – sample size affects reliability. (d) If the distance increases, then the percentage of GM-positive kernels will decrease, because less pollen reaches plants further away.
items.markingKey: (a) 1: distance of the non-GM maize plot from the GM field (5, 25, 50, 100, 200 m). (b) 1: percentage of kernels that test positive for the GM gene (must include how/units). (c) 1 each, variable + reason: any two of maize variety and flowering time (only plants flowering together can cross); number of cobs sampled per plot (20) (sample size affects reliability); wind direction (downwind plots) (pollen is carried by wind); the same test kit (test sensitivity varies). (d) 1 for a testable if/then prediction linking IV and DV, 1 for correct scientific reasoning: If the distance increases, then the percentage of GM-positive kernels will decrease, because less pollen reaches plants further away.

items.stem: Evaluate the use of herbicide-resistant GM soybeans by farmers.
items.answer: Benefits: easy, effective weed control; higher yields; less soil disturbance (no-till farming reduces erosion and CO₂ release). Drawbacks: overuse of one herbicide leading to resistant superweeds; reduced biodiversity of field weeds and insects; seed costs and patents controlling farmers; concerns over herbicide residues. Conclusion: useful with rotation of herbicides and crops and integrated weed management.
items.markingKey: Benefits: easy, effective weed control; higher yields; less soil disturbance (no-till farming reduces erosion and CO₂ release). Drawbacks: overuse of one herbicide leading to resistant superweeds; reduced biodiversity of field weeds and insects; seed costs and patents controlling farmers; concerns over herbicide residues. Conclusion: useful with rotation of herbicides and crops and integrated weed management.

items.stem: Where are adult stem cells found?
items.answer: Bone marrow
items.markingKey: Bone marrow. They make blood cells.

items.stem: Briefly explain why embryonic stem cell research is controversial.
items.answer: Obtaining the cells destroys early embryos, which some people believe have the moral status of a person.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Obtaining the cells destroys early embryos, which some people believe have the moral status of a person. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A clone is an identical copy that will have the same personality and memories." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A clone has the same genes, but environment and experience shape development, so it is a different individual.
items.markingKey: A clone has the same genes, but environment and experience shape development, so it is a different individual. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Arjun recorded the percentage of successful cloned embryos (live births per embryos transferred) in a cattle cloning programme in successive years (three farms).

Year of programme | Success rate / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 4.3 | 4.5 | 4.5
2 | 6.8 | 6.9 | 6.9
3 | 9.1 | 9.2 | 8.8
4 | 11.1 | 11.1 | 11.8
5 | 14.2 | 13.7 | 13.8

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The success rate increased each year but remained low (under about 15%). Technique improvements (handling eggs, timing of fusion and implantation) raise success, but reprogramming an adult nucleus remains unreliable, so many embryos fail.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The success rate increased each year but remained low (under about 15%).; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Technique improvements (handling eggs, timing of fusion and implantation) raise success, but reprogramming an adult nucleus remains unreliable, so many embryos fail.

items.stem: Jonas is investigating how the concentration of plant hormone (auxin) in the growth medium affects root formation in cauliflower tissue culture. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: auxin concentration in the agar (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 mg/dm³)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: auxin concentration in the agar (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 mg/dm³) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Describe how Dolly the sheep was cloned and evaluate the use of animal cloning in agriculture.
items.answer: Udder cell taken from sheep A; egg from sheep B with nucleus removed; nucleus of udder cell inserted (electric shock fuses and stimulates division); embryo grown then implanted in surrogate C; Dolly genetically identical to A. Evaluation: copies high-yield animals quickly; but low success rate, health problems (early ageing debated), reduced genetic diversity → disease risk, ethical and welfare concerns, expensive.
items.markingKey: Udder cell taken from sheep A; egg from sheep B with nucleus removed; nucleus of udder cell inserted (electric shock fuses and stimulates division); embryo grown then implanted in surrogate C; Dolly genetically identical to A. Evaluation: copies high-yield animals quickly; but low success rate, health problems (early ageing debated), reduced genetic diversity → disease risk, ethical and welfare concerns, expensive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Producing an embryo with the patient’s genes to obtain stem cells that will not be rejected"?
options: embryonic stem cell
genetic testing
therapeutic cloning
DNA ligase
items.answer: therapeutic cloning
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of therapeutic cloning.

items.stem: Distinguish between therapeutic cloning and reproductive cloning.
items.answer: Reproductive cloning aims to produce a whole cloned organism; therapeutic cloning produces an early embryo only to harvest stem cells for treatment.
items.markingKey: Reproductive cloning aims to produce a whole cloned organism; therapeutic cloning produces an early embryo only to harvest stem cells for treatment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Stem cell treatments are already available for most diseases." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only a few (e.g. bone marrow transplants) are established; many are experimental or unproven.
items.markingKey: Only a few (e.g. bone marrow transplants) are established; many are experimental or unproven. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Induced pluripotent stem cells (Yamanaka, 2006) as an example, explain avoiding embryo use.
items.answer: Adding four genes to adult skin cells reprogrammed them into stem cells similar to embryonic ones. Nobel Prize 2012; reduces ethical concerns, though there are cancer risks.
items.markingKey: Context (Adding four genes to adult skin cells reprogrammed them into stem cells similar to embryonic ones.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Nobel Prize 2012; reduces ethical concerns, though there are cancer risks. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to avoiding embryo use.

items.stem:
Elena recorded the percentage of successful cloned embryos (live births per embryos transferred) in a cattle cloning programme in successive years (three farms).

Year of programme | Success rate / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 4.6 | 4.3 | 4.4
2 | 6.8 | 6.9 | 6.7
3 | 8.9 | 9.2 | 9.0
4 | 11.9 | 12.0 | 11.8
5 | 13.5 | 13.8 | 14.3

Calculate the percentage change in the mean success rate between 1 and 5.
items.markingKey: M1 means 4.43 and 13.87; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +212.8% (increase).

items.stem: "Cloning endangered animals is a good way to save species from extinction." Discuss.
items.answer: Cloning may help in rare cases, but habitat protection and breeding programmes are far more important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: can increase numbers when very few remain; can restore lost genetic diversity from frozen cells. Arguments against: clones have very low genetic diversity; low success rate and welfare concerns; does not fix habitat loss. Supported judgement: Cloning may help in rare cases, but habitat protection and breeding programmes are far more important. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the concentration of plant hormone (auxin) in the growth medium affects root formation in cauliflower tissue culture. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Sterilise cauliflower florets in dilute bleach; rinse with sterile water; cut 2 mm explants with a sterile scalpel; place 10 in each sterile tube of agar with a set auxin concentration; seal and keep at 25 °C under a 16 h light period; after 3 weeks count explants with roots; repeat three times.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (bleach and ethanol are irritants and flammable; handle scalpels carefully, cutting away from the body). Model: Sterilise cauliflower florets in dilute bleach; rinse with sterile water; cut 2 mm explants with a sterile scalpel; place 10 in each sterile tube of agar with a set auxin concentration; seal and keep at 25 °C under a 16 h light period; after 3 weeks count explants with roots; repeat three times.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "precautionary principle".
items.answer: Taking action to avoid possible harm even if there is no complete scientific proof of harm
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: taking action to avoid possible harm even if there is no complete scientific proof of harm. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between biotechnology in richer countries and biotechnology in poorer countries.
items.answer: Richer countries can afford advanced treatments and regulation; poorer countries may benefit most from cheap solutions (e.g. GM drought-tolerant crops) but have less access and influence.
items.markingKey: Richer countries can afford advanced treatments and regulation; poorer countries may benefit most from cheap solutions (e.g. GM drought-tolerant crops) but have less access and influence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Diego plans to investigate how giving people scientific information affects their acceptance of GM foods, using a survey. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: same survey questions and wording; similar age groups and sample size (50 each); anonymous responses; same time of year
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: same survey questions and wording – wording influences answers; similar age groups and sample size (50 each) – opinions vary with age and samples must be comparable; anonymous responses – people answer more honestly; same time of year – news stories can affect opinions. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: With reference to Henrietta Lacks and HeLa cells (1951), explain how it illustrates informed consent.
items.answer: Cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge became the first immortal cell line, used in polio vaccine and countless studies; her family received no compensation for decades. Her case changed rules on consent and recognition in medical research.
items.markingKey: Context (Cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge became the first immortal cell line, used in polio vaccine and countless studies; her family received no compensation for decades.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Her case changed rules on consent and recognition in medical research. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to informed consent.

items.stem: Discuss the ethical, social and economic implications of offering genetic testing for adult-onset disease (e.g. Huntington’s) to everyone.
items.answer: Benefits: informed life and family planning; early monitoring; research. Concerns: no cure for Huntington’s – psychological distress; privacy and discrimination by insurers/employers; implications for relatives who did not consent; cost to health systems and unequal access; need for counselling and informed consent. Judgement: offer testing with counselling, strong data protection and anti-discrimination laws, not compulsory.
items.markingKey: Benefits: informed life and family planning; early monitoring; research. Concerns: no cure for Huntington’s – psychological distress; privacy and discrimination by insurers/employers; implications for relatives who did not consent; cost to health systems and unequal access; need for counselling and informed consent. Judgement: offer testing with counselling, strong data protection and anti-discrimination laws, not compulsory.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "biopiracy"?
options: Commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge from a community without permission or fair payment
A stem cell from an early embryo that can become any type of cell
Something used to carry a gene into a cell, such as a plasmid or virus
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific base sequence, often leaving sticky ends
items.answer: Commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge from a community without permission or fair payment
items.markingKey: A. "biopiracy" is commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge from a community without permission or fair payment.

items.stem: "If something is scientifically possible, it is ethically acceptable." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Science tells us what can be done; whether it should be done depends on ethical, social and economic judgements.
items.markingKey: Science tells us what can be done; whether it should be done depends on ethical, social and economic judgements. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Noah analysed global survey data on the percentage of people who support GM crops in countries with different average years of schooling (three survey years).

Mean years of schooling | Support for GM crops / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
4 | 46 | 43 | 45
6 | 49 | 52 | 49
8 | 54 | 54 | 55
10 | 61 | 64 | 63
12 | 68 | 65 | 66

Calculate the percentage change in the mean support for GM crops between 4 and 12.
items.markingKey: M1 means 44.7 and 66.3; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +48.5% (increase).

items.stem: Sofia is investigating how giving people scientific information affects their acceptance of GM foods, using a survey. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If people receive factual information and can ask questions, then their acceptance score will increase, because uncertainty and misconceptions are reduced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If people receive factual information and can ask questions, then their acceptance score will increase, because uncertainty and misconceptions are reduced.

items.stem: "Companies should be allowed to patent genes they discover." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Natural genes should not be patentable (as the US Supreme Court ruled in 2013), but specific new technologies using them can be.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: encourages investment in expensive research; protects inventions. Arguments against: genes are natural, not inventions; patents can block research and make tests expensive (e.g. BRCA tests before 2013). Supported judgement: Natural genes should not be patentable (as the US Supreme Court ruled in 2013), but specific new technologies using them can be. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "DNA ligase"?
options: A stem cell found in tissues such as bone marrow that can form a limited range of cells
DNA that combines genetic material from two different sources
Changing the genome of an organism by inserting a gene from another organism
An enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together
items.answer: An enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together
items.markingKey: D. "DNA ligase" is an enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gene flow"?
options: DNA that combines genetic material from two different sources
A stem cell from an early embryo that can become any type of cell
The transfer of genes between populations, e.g. by pollen from GM crops to wild relatives
A genetically identical copy of an organism, cell or gene
items.answer: The transfer of genes between populations, e.g. by pollen from GM crops to wild relatives
items.markingKey: C. "gene flow" is the transfer of genes between populations, e.g. by pollen from GM crops to wild relatives.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "adult stem cell"?
options: A legal right to be the only one to make or sell an invention for a period of time
Something used to carry a gene into a cell, such as a plasmid or virus
A stem cell found in tissues such as bone marrow that can form a limited range of cells
A small circular loop of DNA in bacteria, used as a vector
items.answer: A stem cell found in tissues such as bone marrow that can form a limited range of cells
items.markingKey: C. "adult stem cell" is a stem cell found in tissues such as bone marrow that can form a limited range of cells.

items.stem: Briefly explain why access to biotechnology can increase global inequality.
items.answer: Expensive treatments and technologies are first available in richer countries, while poorer countries may lack infrastructure and funding.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Expensive treatments and technologies are first available in richer countries, while poorer countries may lack infrastructure and funding. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why sticky ends make recombinant DNA possible.
items.answer: The single-stranded overhangs from the same restriction enzyme have complementary base sequences, so they hydrogen-bond together before ligase seals them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The single-stranded overhangs from the same restriction enzyme have complementary base sequences, so they hydrogen-bond together before ligase seals them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why some people oppose GM foods even though no harm to health has been shown.
items.answer: Concerns about long-term ecological effects, corporate control of seeds and patents, labelling and choice, and ethical objections to “unnatural” changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Concerns about long-term ecological effects, corporate control of seeds and patents, labelling and choice, and ethical objections to “unnatural” changes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells.
items.answer: Embryonic stem cells can become any cell type but raise ethical issues; adult stem cells are less ethically controversial but can only form a limited range of cells.
items.markingKey: Embryonic stem cells can become any cell type but raise ethical issues; adult stem cells are less ethically controversial but can only form a limited range of cells. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between biotechnology in poorer countries and biotechnology in richer countries.
items.answer: Richer countries can afford advanced treatments and regulation; poorer countries may benefit most from cheap solutions (e.g. GM drought-tolerant crops) but have less access and influence.
items.markingKey: Richer countries can afford advanced treatments and regulation; poorer countries may benefit most from cheap solutions (e.g. GM drought-tolerant crops) but have less access and influence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why bacteria are useful for producing human proteins.
items.answer: They reproduce rapidly, use the same genetic code, are easy to grow in fermenters and have plasmids that can carry new genes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They reproduce rapidly, use the same genetic code, are easy to grow in fermenters and have plasmids that can carry new genes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "GM crops are always bad for the environment." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some reduce pesticide use and allow less tillage, but others may encourage more herbicide use; effects depend on the crop and management.
items.markingKey: Some reduce pesticide use and allow less tillage, but others may encourage more herbicide use; effects depend on the crop and management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the concentration of plant hormone (auxin) in the growth medium affects root formation in cauliflower tissue culture, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: temperature and light.
items.answer: affect growth
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (temperature and light) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: affect growth. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem:
Lukas analysed global survey data on the percentage of people who support GM crops in countries with different average years of schooling (three survey years).

Mean years of schooling | Support for GM crops / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
4 | 43 | 42 | 43
6 | 50 | 49 | 48
8 | 52 | 52 | 56
10 | 58 | 59 | 57
12 | 62 | 63 | 67

State the mean years of schooling at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 12; range = 5 %; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 12; 1 range = max − min = 67 − 62 = 5 %; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.answer: Anomaly: 147 (trial 2 at 40 ng); mean = 109.0

items.stem: "Eating GM food will change your DNA." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Digestion breaks down DNA from all foods into nucleotides; it is not incorporated into your genome.
items.markingKey: Digestion breaks down DNA from all foods into nucleotides; it is not incorporated into your genome. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Dolly the sheep (Roslin Institute, 1996) as an example, explain cloning from adult cells.
items.answer: The nucleus of an udder cell was fused with an enucleated egg; after 277 attempts, Dolly was born. It proved specialised adult cells contain all the genes needed to make a whole animal.
items.markingKey: Context (The nucleus of an udder cell was fused with an enucleated egg; after 277 attempts, Dolly was born.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It proved specialised adult cells contain all the genes needed to make a whole animal. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cloning from adult cells.

items.stem: Briefly describe Henrietta Lacks and HeLa cells (1951) and explain what it reveals about informed consent.
items.answer: Cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge became the first immortal cell line, used in polio vaccine and countless studies; her family received no compensation for decades. Her case changed rules on consent and recognition in medical research.
items.markingKey: Context (Cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge became the first immortal cell line, used in polio vaccine and countless studies; her family received no compensation for decades.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Her case changed rules on consent and recognition in medical research. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to informed consent.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the temperature of the heat-shock step affects the number of E. coli K-12 cells that take up a plasmid carrying a fluorescence gene. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): use a non-pathogenic strain; aseptic technique; UV light can damage eyes – use UV-protective glasses; autoclave all waste. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. use a non-pathogenic strain; aseptic technique; UV light can damage eyes – use UV-protective glasses; autoclave all waste); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Golden Rice should be grown widely in countries with vitamin A deficiency."
items.answer: Golden Rice is a valuable tool alongside supplements and dietary diversity, given strong evidence of safety and benefit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: could prevent hundreds of thousands of cases of childhood blindness and death; cheap, fits existing diets. Arguments against: opposition to GM; possible cross-pollination; supplements and diverse diets are alternatives. Supported judgement: Golden Rice is a valuable tool alongside supplements and dietary diversity, given strong evidence of safety and benefit. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Mateo plans an investigation into how the concentration of plant hormone (auxin) in the growth medium affects root formation in cauliflower tissue culture. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (auxin concentration in the agar (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 mg/dm³)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how giving people scientific information affects their acceptance of GM foods, using a survey. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Recruit three similar groups of 50 adults with informed consent; give each group one type of information; ask the same 10 questions anonymously; calculate mean acceptance score for each group; compare using means and ranges.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, anonymous data stored securely). Model: Recruit three similar groups of 50 adults with informed consent; give each group one type of information; ask the same 10 questions anonymously; calculate mean acceptance score for each group; compare using means and ranges.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together"?
options: plasmid
DNA ligase
restriction enzyme
adult stem cell
items.answer: DNA ligase
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of DNA ligase.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "monoculture".
items.answer: Growing one crop variety over a large area
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: growing one crop variety over a large area. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "adult stem cell".
items.answer: A stem cell found in tissues such as bone marrow that can form a limited range of cells

items.stem: Explain why patents on genetically modified seeds are controversial.
items.answer: They reward innovation, but farmers may be unable to save seed, increasing costs, and companies gain control over food supply.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They reward innovation, but farmers may be unable to save seed, increasing costs, and companies gain control over food supply. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a restriction enzyme and DNA ligase.
items.answer: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific sequences; DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together.
items.markingKey: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific sequences; DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a Bt crop and a herbicide-resistant crop.
items.answer: A Bt crop produces its own insecticide; a herbicide-resistant crop survives being sprayed with weedkiller, so weeds can be killed.
items.markingKey: A Bt crop produces its own insecticide; a herbicide-resistant crop survives being sprayed with weedkiller, so weeds can be killed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Bt cotton in India (from 2002), explain how it illustrates benefits and limits of GM crops.
items.answer: Bt cotton spread to over 90% of India’s cotton area; yields rose and insecticide use fell at first, but pink bollworm later evolved resistance. It shows both the benefits of GM traits and how evolution can reduce them without careful management.
items.markingKey: Context (Bt cotton spread to over 90% of India’s cotton area; yields rose and insecticide use fell at first, but pink bollworm later evolved resistance.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows both the benefits of GM traits and how evolution can reduce them without careful management. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to benefits and limits of GM crops.

items.stem:
Maya recorded the percentage of successful cloned embryos (live births per embryos transferred) in a cattle cloning programme in successive years (three farms).

Year of programme | Success rate / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 4.6
2 | 7.1 | 7.0 | 7.2
3 | 9.5 | 9.3 | 9.6
4 | 11.6 | 11.7 | 12.0
5 | 14.4 | 14.0 | 14.6

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The success rate increased each year but remained low (under about 15%). Technique improvements (handling eggs, timing of fusion and implantation) raise success, but reprogramming an adult nucleus remains unreliable, so many embryos fail.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The success rate increased each year but remained low (under about 15%).; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Technique improvements (handling eggs, timing of fusion and implantation) raise success, but reprogramming an adult nucleus remains unreliable, so many embryos fail.

items.stem: With reference to Recombinant insulin (Genentech, 1978–1982), explain how it illustrates genetic engineering in medicine.
items.answer: Scientists inserted synthetic human insulin genes into E. coli; in 1982 Humulin became the first genetically engineered medicine approved for humans. It replaced animal insulin and showed that GM bacteria could make human proteins safely at scale.
items.markingKey: Context (Scientists inserted synthetic human insulin genes into E. coli; in 1982 Humulin became the first genetically engineered medicine approved for humans.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Gene editing with CRISPR should be allowed to correct genetic diseases in human embryos."
items.answer: Research should continue, but heritable embryo editing should wait for proven safety and broad social agreement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: could eliminate severe inherited diseases (e.g. Huntington’s); prevents suffering in future generations. Arguments against: changes are inherited by all descendants – unknown long-term effects; off-target edits; could lead to “designer babies” and inequality. Supported judgement: Research should continue, but heritable embryo editing should wait for proven safety and broad social agreement.

items.stem: "Cloning endangered animals is a good way to save species from extinction." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Cloning may help in rare cases, but habitat protection and breeding programmes are far more important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: can increase numbers when very few remain; can restore lost genetic diversity from frozen cells. Arguments against: clones have very low genetic diversity; low success rate and welfare concerns; does not fix habitat loss. Supported judgement: Cloning may help in rare cases, but habitat protection and breeding programmes are far more important.
